p.src: In the sixth month of summer, the second year of Zhangwu, Lu Xun of Eastern Wu crushed the Shu army at Xiaoting and Yiling; the First Emperor fled back to Baidi, where Zhao Yun led the troops in holding the defenses. Ma Liang suddenly arrived. Seeing that the great army had already been defeated, he bitterly regretted coming too late and reported Zhuge Liang's words to the First Emperor. The First Emperor sighed, “Had I heeded the Chancellor's counsel earlier, I would not have suffered today's defeat! How can I ever return to Chengdu and face my ministers now?” He therefore issued an edict to remain at Baidi and had the posthouse converted into the Palace of Yong'an. When told that Feng Xi, Zhang Nan, Fu Tong, Cheng Ji, Shamoke, and the others had all died in the royal cause, the First Emperor grieved without cease. A close attendant further reported, “Huang Quan has led the troops north of the river over to Wei. Your Majesty should hand his family over to the authorities for punishment.” The First Emperor said, “Huang Quan was cut off by the Wu forces on the north bank. With no road home, he had no choice but to surrender to Wei. It is I who have failed Quan, not Quan who has failed me. Why punish his family?” He continued to provide them with stipends of grain for their support.

p.src: Now Huang Quan, having surrendered to Wei, was brought by the generals before Cao Pi. Cao Pi said, “In submitting to me today, do you mean to emulate Chen Ping and Han Xin?” Huang Quan tearfully replied, “The Emperor of Shu treated me with extraordinary favor and commanded me to oversee the armies north of the river, but Lu Xun cut me off. I had no way back to Shu and could not surrender to Wu, so I came to seek refuge with Your Majesty. As a defeated general, I count escape from death a blessing. How dare I aspire to emulate the men of old?” Cao Pi was delighted and appointed Huang Quan General Who Guards the South. Huang Quan firmly declined the appointment. Suddenly a close attendant reported, “A spy has arrived from Shu saying that the ruler of Shu has put Huang Quan's entire family to death.” Huang Quan said, “The ruler of Shu and I trusted each other with perfect sincerity. p.src: Cao Pi asked Jia Xu, “I wish to unite the realm. Should I take Shu first, or Wu first?” Jia Xu replied, “Liu Bei possesses heroic talent, and Zhuge Liang excels at governing the state. Sun Quan of Eastern Wu can discern truth from deception, while Lu Xun now has troops posted at strategic strongholds beyond river and lake. Neither realm can be swiftly taken by stratagem. In my judgment, none among our generals is a match for Sun Quan or Liu Bei. Even if Your Majesty were to descend upon them in heavenly might, complete success could not be assured. We should merely hold our ground and await changes within the two states.” Cao Pi said, “I have already sent three great armies against Wu. How could they fail to prevail?” Liu Ye, the Imperial Secretary, said, “Lu Xun of Eastern Wu has just routed seven hundred thousand Shu troops. All ranks are united, and the rivers and lakes provide formidable barriers; Wu cannot be subdued quickly. Lu Xun is full of stratagems and will surely be prepared.” Cao Pi said, “You formerly urged me to attack Wu, yet now you seek to dissuade me. Why?” Liu Ye replied, “Circumstances have changed. Then, Eastern Wu had suffered repeated defeats at Shu's hands and its strength was broken, so it could be attacked; but now, after winning a complete victory, its ardor has increased a hundredfold, and it must not yet be attacked.” Cao Pi said, “My mind is settled. Say no more.” He then led the imperial guards in person to support the armies on the three routes. Scouts soon reported that Eastern Wu was already prepared: Lü Fan had been ordered to oppose Cao Xiu, Zhuge Jin to hold Cao Zhen at Nanjun, and Zhu Huan to block Ruxu against Cao Ren. Liu Ye said, “Since they are prepared, going there will likely be useless.” Cao Pi would not listen and led his army onward.

p.src: Now the Wu general Zhu Huan was only twenty-seven years old, but possessed exceptional courage and strategy, and Sun Quan held him in great favor. At that time he commanded the forces at Ruxu. Hearing that Cao Ren was leading a great army to seize Xianxi, Zhu Huan dispatched nearly all his troops to defend Xianxi, leaving only five thousand horsemen to guard the city. Suddenly came word that Cao Ren had ordered the general Chang Diao, together with Zhuge Qian and Wang Shuang, to rush upon Ruxu with fifty thousand elite troops. Fear showed on every soldier's face. Zhu Huan gripped his sword and said, “Victory and defeat depend upon the commander, not upon the number of troops. The art of war says: ‘Even when an invading force is twice as numerous and the defending force only half its size, the defenders can still defeat the invaders.’ Cao Ren has now marched a thousand li, and both men and horses are exhausted. We hold this high-walled city together, with the great river before us to the south and rugged mountains behind us to the north. We await the weary at our ease and, as hosts, command the invaders: this is a position that ensures victory in every battle. Even if Cao Pi came in person, he would scarcely merit concern, much less Cao Ren and his men!” He then ordered the soldiers to lower their banners and silence their drums, making it appear that no one defended the city.

p.src: Now Chang Diao, vanguard general of Wei, led his elite troops to seize Ruxu. From afar he saw no soldiers or horses upon the walls. Chang Diao urged his troops rapidly onward. When they drew near the city, a cannon boomed and banners rose everywhere. Zhu Huan galloped out with his saber held crosswise and charged straight at Chang Diao. Before three bouts had passed, Zhu Huan struck Chang Diao from his horse with a single blow. The Wu troops seized the advantage and charged, utterly routing the Wei army and killing countless men. Zhu Huan won a great victory and captured innumerable banners, weapons, and warhorses. Cao Ren arrived behind them with his troops, only to be attacked by Wu forces issuing from Xianxi. Cao Ren suffered a crushing defeat and withdrew. Returning to the ruler of Wei, he reported the disaster in full. Cao Pi was greatly alarmed. While they were deliberating, a scout suddenly reported, “Cao Zhen and Xiahou Shang surrounded Nanjun, but Lu Xun had an ambush within and Zhuge Jin another without. Attacked from both sides, they suffered a great defeat.” Before he had finished, another scout reported, “Cao Xiu, too, has been routed by Lü Fan.” Learning that all three armies had been defeated, Cao Pi heaved a sigh and said, “I refused to heed Jia Xu and Liu Ye, and now this defeat has indeed befallen me!” It was summer, and a great epidemic was raging. Six or seven soldiers in every ten, cavalry and infantry alike, died, so Cao Pi led the army back to Luoyang. From that time onward, Wu and Wei were at odds.

p.src: Now the First Emperor fell ill at the Palace of Yong'an and could not rise; his condition steadily worsened. By the fourth month of summer, the third year of Zhangwu, he knew the sickness had spread throughout his limbs. He wept again for his two brothers, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, and his illness deepened. His sight grew dim, and he could not bear to see his attendants. He dismissed everyone around him and lay alone upon the imperial couch. Suddenly a chill wind arose, making the lamp flicker; it went out, then flared up again. Beneath its light he saw two men standing in attendance. The First Emperor angrily exclaimed, “My mind is troubled, and I ordered you all to withdraw. Why have you returned?” He rebuked them, but they did not leave. The First Emperor rose and looked: the man in the place of honor was Yun-chang, and the other was Yi-de. Greatly startled, he said, “So my two brothers still live!” Yun-chang replied, “We are not men, but spirits. Because we never betrayed faith or righteousness in life, the Lord of Heaven has decreed that we both become gods. The time when our elder brother shall be reunited with us is not far away.” The First Emperor seized hold of them and wept bitterly. Suddenly he awoke with a start, and his two brothers were gone. He at once summoned his attendants and questioned them. It was then the third watch. The First Emperor sighed, “I shall not remain long in this world!” He therefore sent an envoy to Chengdu, summoning Chancellor Zhuge Liang, Imperial Secretariat Director Li Yan, and the others to hasten by night to the Palace of Yong'an and receive his final commands. Zhuge Liang and the others came to the Palace of Yong'an to see the Emperor, accompanied by the First Emperor's second son, Liu Yong, Prince of Lu, and Liu Li, Prince of Liang; Crown Prince Liu Shan remained behind to guard Chengdu.

p.src: Now Kongming came to the Yong'an Palace and, seeing the First Emperor gravely ill, hastily prostrated himself beside the imperial couch. The First Emperor commanded Kongming to sit beside the imperial couch, stroked his back, and said, “Since gaining you as my chancellor, I have fortunately established an imperial enterprise; but little did I expect that, through my shallow judgment and failure to heed your counsel, I would bring defeat upon myself. Regret and remorse have made me ill, and death may come at any moment. My heir is weak, so I have no choice but to entrust the great affairs of state to you.” When he had finished, tears streamed over his face. Kongming also wept and said, “May Your Majesty take good care of your sacred person and fulfill the hopes of all beneath Heaven!” The First Emperor looked all around and saw Ma Su, younger brother of Ma Liang, standing nearby; he ordered Ma Su to withdraw for the moment. After Ma Su had gone out, the First Emperor asked Kongming, “What do you think of Ma Su's abilities, Chancellor?” Kongming replied, “He too is an outstanding talent of our age.” The First Emperor said, “That is not so. In my judgment, his words exceed his actual ability, and he must not be entrusted with great responsibilities. You should examine him most carefully.” Having given these instructions, he summoned all the ministers into the hall, took paper and brush, wrote his last edict, and handed it to Kongming with a sigh: “I am not a learned man and know only the broad principles. The sage said: ‘When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good.’ I had intended to destroy the Cao rebels together with you all and restore the House of Han; unhappily, I must leave you midway. I ask you, Chancellor, to deliver this edict to Crown Prince Shan and tell him not to regard it as commonplace counsel. In all matters, I look to you, Chancellor!”

p.src: Kongming and the others wept and bowed to the ground, saying, “May Your Majesty rest and preserve your sacred person! We shall exert ourselves like dogs and horses to repay Your Majesty's grace in recognizing our worth.” The First Emperor ordered the attendants to help Kongming to his feet. Covering his tears with one hand and grasping Kongming's hand with the other, he said, “I am dying now! I have words from my innermost heart to tell you!” Kongming said, “What is Your Majesty's sacred command?” The First Emperor wept and said, “Your talent is ten times that of Cao Pi. You will surely bring peace to the realm, establish the state, and in the end accomplish the great cause. If my heir is worthy of your support, then support him; but if he proves unworthy, you may become lord of Chengdu yourself.” On hearing this, sweat poured over Kongming's whole body, and he knew not what to do with his hands or feet. Weeping, he bowed to the ground and said, “How could I dare do otherwise than exhaust the strength of all my limbs, prove my loyal constancy, and continue unto death!” With that, he struck his head upon the ground until it bled. The First Emperor again asked Kongming to sit upon the couch, then called Liu Yong, Prince of Lu, and Liu Li, Prince of Liang, forward and instructed them: “All of you remember my words. After my death, you three brothers must serve the Chancellor as a father and never treat him with neglect.” Having said this, he ordered the two princes to bow together to Kongming. When the two princes had finished bowing, Kongming said, “Even if my liver and brains were smeared upon the ground, how could I ever repay the grace of being so understood and valued!”

p.src: The First Emperor told the assembled officials, “I have entrusted my orphaned heir to the Chancellor and ordered my successor to serve him as a father. None of you must treat him with neglect and thus disappoint my hopes.” Then he charged Zhao Yun: “You and I have accompanied one another through hardship and peril until this day. I never thought we would part in this place. Remember our old friendship, watch over my sons at all times, and do not fail my words.” Zhao Yun wept and bowed, saying, “How could I dare fail to render the service of a dog or horse!” The First Emperor again addressed the assembled officials: “My ministers, I cannot give each of you a separate final charge. I pray that you all take good care of yourselves.” When he had finished speaking, the Emperor passed away at the age of sixty-three. p.src: The ministers finished reading the edict. Kongming said, “A state cannot be without a sovereign for a single day; I ask that the succeeding lord be enthroned to continue the Han line.” Crown Prince Shan was therefore enthroned as emperor, and the era name was changed to Jianxing. Zhuge Liang was additionally enfeoffed as Marquis of Wuxiang and appointed Governor of Yizhou. The First Emperor was buried at Huiling and given the posthumous title Emperor Zhaolie. Empress Wu was honored as Empress Dowager. Lady Gan was honored as Empress Zhaolie. Lady Mi was also posthumously honored as empress. The ministers were promoted and rewarded, and a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm.

p.src: Wei scouts soon learned of these events and reported them in the Central Plains. A close attendant reported the news to the ruler of Wei. Cao Pi rejoiced greatly and said, “Liu Bei is dead; I have no more cause for concern. Why not take advantage of the absence of a ruler in his state and raise an army against it?” Jia Xu remonstrated, “Upon Liu Bei's death, he will surely have entrusted his orphaned heir to Zhuge Liang. Moved by Liu Bei's grace in recognizing his worth, Zhuge Liang will surely devote his heart and all his strength to supporting the succeeding lord. Your Majesty must not attack them hastily.” While he was speaking, a man suddenly strode boldly out from the ranks and said, “If we do not advance now, what other time are we waiting for?” All looked and saw that it was Sima Yi. Cao Pi was delighted and immediately asked Sima Yi for a plan. Sima Yi said, “If we raise only the armies of the central realm, it will be difficult to gain a swift victory. We must employ five great armies to attack from all sides, leaving Zhuge Liang unable to aid both front and rear. Only then can we accomplish our design.”

p.src: Cao Pi asked what the five routes were. Sima Yi said, “A letter may be written and an envoy sent to Kebineng, king of the Xianbei in Liaodong. p.src: In the eighth month of autumn, the first year of Jianxing, an urgent report suddenly arrived from the frontier: “Wei has mobilized five great armies to seize Western Shu. On the first route, Cao Zhen, as Commander-in-Chief, is leading one hundred thousand troops against Yangping Pass; on the second, the turncoat general Meng Da is bringing one hundred thousand troops from Shangyong to invade Hanzhong; on the third, Sun Quan of Eastern Wu is raising one hundred thousand elite troops to take Xiakou and enter Shu; on the fourth, Meng Huo, king of the southern tribes, is leading one hundred thousand tribal soldiers against the four commanderies of Yizhou; and on the fifth, Kebineng, king of the western tribes, is leading one hundred thousand Qiang troops against Xiping Pass. These five armies present a grave danger. The Prime Minister was informed beforehand, but for some unknown reason he has not appeared to conduct affairs for several days.” On hearing this, the Latter Emperor was greatly alarmed and immediately sent a close attendant bearing an edict to summon Kongming to court. Half a day later the envoy returned and reported, “The servants at the Prime Minister’s residence say that he has fallen ill and will not come out.” The Latter Emperor grew still more anxious. The next day he ordered Dong Yun, Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gate, and Du Qiong, Grand Master of Remonstrance, to go to the Prime Minister’s bedside and tell him of this grave crisis. When Dong Yun and Du Qiong reached the Prime Minister’s residence, neither was allowed inside. Du Qiong said, “The Former Emperor entrusted his orphaned heir to the Prime Minister. Now, just as His Majesty has ascended the throne, Cao Pi has sent five armies across our borders. The military situation is desperately urgent—why does the Prime Minister feign illness and refuse to appear?” After a long while, a gate official conveyed the Prime Minister’s order: “My health has improved somewhat. Tomorrow morning I shall attend the government hall to deliberate on affairs.” Dong Yun and Du Qiong returned with sighs. The next day, many officials again came to wait before the Prime Minister’s residence. But from morning until evening, he still did not appear. The officials were filled with alarm and had no choice but to disperse. Du Qiong entered the palace and memorialized to the Latter Emperor, “I beg Your Majesty to go in person to the Prime Minister’s residence and ask his counsel.” The Latter Emperor at once led the officials into the inner palace and informed the Empress Dowager. The Empress Dowager was greatly shocked and said, “Why is the Prime Minister behaving in this manner? He is betraying the trust placed in him by the Former Emperor! I shall go there myself.” Dong Yun memorialized, “Your Majesty the Empress Dowager must not go there lightly. I believe the Prime Minister must have some profound design. Let His Majesty go first. If the Prime Minister should still prove remiss, it will not be too late for Your Majesty to summon him to the ancestral temple and question him there.” The Empress Dowager accepted his counsel.

p.src: The next day, the Latter Emperor went in person with his imperial carriage to the Prime Minister’s residence. When the gate official saw the imperial carriage arrive, he hurriedly prostrated himself on the ground in welcome. The Latter Emperor asked, “Where is the Prime Minister?” The gate official replied, “I do not know where he is. We have only the Prime Minister’s strict order to keep all the officials outside and admit no one without permission.” The Latter Emperor alighted and proceeded on foot. Entering the third gate alone, he saw Kongming leaning upon a bamboo staff beside a small pond, watching the fish. The Latter Emperor stood behind him for a long while before saying gently, “Is the Prime Minister quite at ease?” Kongming looked around and, seeing the Latter Emperor, hastily cast aside his staff, prostrated himself, and said, “Your servant deserves ten thousand deaths!” The Latter Emperor helped him rise and asked, “Now Cao Pi has divided his forces into five armies and is pressing urgently across our borders. Why does my father the Prime Minister refuse to leave his residence and attend to affairs?” Kongming laughed heartily, supported the Latter Emperor into an inner chamber, and, once they were seated, memorialized, “How could I fail to know that the five armies have come? I was not watching the fish; I was pondering a matter.” The Latter Emperor said, “What is to be done?” Kongming replied, “Kebineng, king of the Qiang; Meng Huo, king of the southern tribes; the turncoat general Meng Da; and the Wei general Cao Zhen—I have already repelled all four of these armies. Why need Your Majesty worry?”

p.src: When the Latter Emperor heard this, he was both astonished and delighted. “My father the Prime Minister truly possesses designs unfathomable even to spirits and gods! I beg to hear how you have contrived to repel them.” Kongming replied, “The Former Emperor entrusted Your Majesty to me. How could I dare neglect my duty for so much as a morning or evening? The officials in Chengdu do not comprehend the subtleties of warfare, whose supreme value lies in making one’s designs unfathomable. How could such matters be divulged to others? I knew beforehand that Kebineng, king of the western tribes, would lead troops against Xiping Pass. I considered that Ma Chao’s family had lived in Western Shu for generations, that he had long enjoyed the allegiance of the Qiang people, and that they revered him as the General of Divine Might. I therefore sent a man ahead with all speed, galloping day and night with a dispatch ordering Ma Chao to guard Xiping Pass closely. He was to place four detachments in ambush and rotate them daily to resist the enemy. Thus there is no need to worry about that army. As for Meng Huo of the southern tribes, whose troops are invading the four commanderies, I likewise sent an urgent dispatch ordering Wei Yan to lead an army out on the left and enter on the right, then out on the right and enter on the left, thus creating a feint. The tribal soldiers rely only on courage and strength, and their minds are deeply suspicious. When they see deceptive movements, they will certainly not dare advance. Thus that army, too, gives no cause for concern. I also learned that Meng Da was leading troops out toward Hanzhong. Meng Da and Li Yan once swore friendship unto death. When I returned to Chengdu, I left Li Yan to guard the Yong’an Palace. I have written a letter in Li Yan’s own hand and had it delivered to Meng Da. Meng Da will surely plead illness and refuse to march, thereby sapping the army’s spirit. Thus that army also gives no cause for concern. I further learned that Cao Zhen was leading troops against Yangping Pass. The terrain there is steep and rugged and can readily be defended. I have ordered Zhao Yun to lead an army to hold the pass and on no account offer battle. When Cao Zhen sees that our army will not come out, he will soon withdraw of his own accord. None of these four armies need trouble us. Yet, fearing these measures might not provide complete security, I also secretly ordered the two generals Guan Xing and Zhang Bao each to lead thirty thousand troops and station themselves at strategic points, ready to support every front. None of these deployments passed through Chengdu, and so no one here became aware of them. Only the army of Eastern Wu remains, and it may not move at all. If the other four armies prevail and the situation in Shu becomes critical, Wu will certainly come to attack us; but if those four armies fail, why would Wu consent to move? I judge that Sun Quan, remembering his resentment over Cao Pi’s three-pronged invasion of Wu, will certainly refuse to heed him. Even so, we must send an eloquent man straight to Eastern Wu to explain the advantages and perils, and thus induce Wu to withdraw first. Then what need is there to worry about the other four armies? It is only because I have not yet found a man capable of persuading Wu that I have been hesitating. Why did Your Majesty trouble yourself to come here in person?” The Latter Emperor said, “The Empress Dowager also wished to come and see my father the Prime Minister. Now that I have heard your words, it is as though I have awakened from a dream. What cause have I to worry any longer?”

p.src: Kongming drank several cups with the Latter Lord, then escorted him out of the residence. All the officials stood gathered outside the gate and saw that the Latter Lord's face bore a look of delight. The Latter Lord took leave of Kongming, mounted the imperial carriage, and returned to court. The assembled officials were all bewildered and uncertain. Among the officials, Kongming noticed one man laughing up at the heavens, his face likewise bright with joy. Kongming looked closely and saw that it was Deng Zhi, courtesy name Bomiao, a native of Xinye in Yiyang. He currently held the office of Minister of Revenue, and was a descendant of Deng Yu, Grand Marshal of the Han. Kongming secretly ordered someone to ask Deng Zhi to remain behind. The other officials all dispersed. Kongming invited Deng Zhi into his study and asked him, “Now that Shu, Wei, and Wu stand divided as three rival kingdoms, if we wish to conquer the other two and restore unity through a revival of the Han, which should we attack first?” Deng Zhi replied, “In my humble opinion, although Wei is a traitor to the Han, its power is immense and cannot readily be shaken. We must proceed against it slowly and with patience. His Majesty has only just ascended the throne, and the people's allegiance is not yet settled. We should therefore ally ourselves with Eastern Wu and form a bond as close as lips and teeth, wiping away the former enmity left from the late Emperor's time. This is the sound policy for the years ahead. I do not know whether this accords with Your Excellency's august judgment.” Kongming laughed heartily and said, “I have long been thinking the same, but had not found the right man. Today, at last, I have found him!” Deng Zhi asked, “For what purpose does Your Excellency require such a man?” Kongming replied, “I wish to send someone to forge an alliance with Eastern Wu. Since you have understood my intention so clearly, you will surely acquit yourself without disgracing your sovereign's commission. No one but you can undertake this mission to Wu.” Deng Zhi said, “My humble talents and wisdom are shallow; I fear I am unequal to so weighty a charge.” Kongming said, “Tomorrow I shall report the matter to the Emperor and request that you, Bomiao, undertake the journey. You must not refuse.” Deng Zhi assented and withdrew. The next day, Kongming obtained the Latter Lord's approval and dispatched Deng Zhi to persuade Eastern Wu. Deng Zhi took formal leave and set out toward Eastern Wu. Thus it was said:
